topics.title: Design a Key-Value Store
topics.description: Understanding distributed key-value databases, CAP theorem trade-offs, partitioning, replication, and storage engine design.

subtopics.title: Key-Value Store
subtopics.theory:
1️⃣ Key-Value Store

✅ Definition

A Key-Value Store is a distributed database that stores data as a pair:

Key → Value

Key: unique identifier

Value: arbitrary data (string, JSON, blob, binary)

It is optimized for fast key-based access.



✅ Why It Is Needed

Handle massive scale (millions of QPS)

Low latency reads and writes

Simple data model

Horizontal scaling



✅ Important Points

Schema-less

No joins

No complex queries

Data accessed only via key

Designed for distribution



✅ Advantages

Very fast (O(1) access average)

Scales horizontally easily

High availability

Simple to implement



❌ Disadvantages

Cannot query by value

No relational constraints

Conflict resolution complexity

Possible stale reads

subtopics.title: CAP Theorem
subtopics.theory:
2️⃣ CAP Theorem



✅ Definition

In a distributed system, you can guarantee at most two of three:

Consistency

Availability

Partition Tolerance



✅ Important Understanding

Partition tolerance is mandatory in distributed systems.

So real trade-off:

Consistency vs Availability



CP System

Guarantees consistency

May reject requests during partition



AP System

Guarantees availability

May return stale data

subtopics.title: Consistency Models
subtopics.theory:
3️⃣ Consistency Models



✅ Strong Consistency

Read always returns latest write

Higher latency

Requires coordination



✅ Eventual Consistency

Reads may be stale

System converges eventually

Most scalable option



✅ Weak Consistency

No guarantees

Fastest

subtopics.title: Data Partitioning
subtopics.theory:
4️⃣ Data Partitioning



✅ Definition

Dividing dataset across multiple nodes.



✅ Why Needed

Scale storage

Scale traffic

Avoid single-node bottleneck



Methods

Hash-Based Partitioning

hash(key) % number_of_nodes

Problem: massive reshuffling when nodes change.

subtopics.title: Consistent Hashing
subtopics.theory:
5️⃣ Consistent Hashing



✅ Definition

Partitioning technique that minimizes data movement when nodes join/leave.



How It Works

Nodes placed on hash ring

Keys hashed to ring

Assigned to nearest clockwise node



Virtual Nodes

One physical node mapped multiple times

Improves load balance



Advantage

Only small % of keys move when cluster changes.

subtopics.title: Replication
subtopics.theory:
6️⃣ Replication



✅ Definition

Storing multiple copies of data.



Why Needed

Fault tolerance

High availability

Read scaling



Replication Factor (N)

Number of copies of each key.

Example:

N = 3

Data stored on 3 nodes.



Replication Models

Leader–Follower

One leader handles writes

Followers replicate



Leaderless (Dynamo Style)

Any node can accept write

Uses quorum



Trade-Off

More replicas → better durability
More replicas → more coordination cost

subtopics.title: Quorum Mechanism
subtopics.theory:
7️⃣ Quorum Mechanism



Parameters

N = total replicas

W = write acknowledgments

R = read acknowledgments

Rule for strong consistency:

R + W > N



Example

N = 3
W = 2
R = 2

At least one overlapping replica ensures latest value.



Trade-Off

Higher R/W → higher latency
Lower R/W → higher availability

subtopics.title: Versioning
subtopics.theory:
8️⃣ Versioning



✅ Definition

Attaching version metadata to each value.

Used to:

Detect conflicts

Maintain causality



Techniques

Timestamp

Simple

Risk of clock skew



Vector Clock

Tracks causality

Detects concurrent updates

More accurate

subtopics.title: Conflict Resolution
subtopics.theory:
9️⃣ Conflict Resolution



When It Happens

Concurrent writes

Network partition



Techniques

Last Write Wins (LWW)

Newest timestamp wins.

Risk: data loss.



Vector Clock Resolution

Detects concurrent versions.



Application Merge

Business logic decides.

subtopics.title: Write Path
subtopics.theory:
🔟 Write Path (Detailed Flow)



Client sends PUT

Coordinator node receives request

Write stored in commit log (durability)

Written to Memtable

Sent to N replicas

Wait for W acknowledgments

Return success

subtopics.title: Read Path
subtopics.theory:
1️⃣1️⃣ Read Path (Detailed Flow)



Client sends GET

Coordinator selects R replicas

Retrieves versions

Picks latest version

Performs read repair if needed

Returns value

subtopics.title: Failure Handling
subtopics.theory:
1️⃣2️⃣ Failure Handling



Temporary Failure

Hinted handoff stores writes

Delivered later



Permanent Failure

Data rebuilt from replicas

Rebalancing triggered



Gossip Protocol

Nodes exchange state periodically to detect failures.

subtopics.title: Storage Engine
subtopics.theory:
1️⃣3️⃣ Storage Engine



Most distributed KV stores use:

LSM Tree (Log Structured Merge Tree)



Write Flow

Write → Commit Log

Write → Memtable (in memory)

Flush to SSTable (disk)

Background compaction merges files



Components

Memtable

In-memory sorted structure.



SSTable

Immutable disk file.



Compaction

Merging old SSTables.



Bloom Filter

Probabilistic structure to check if key exists.
Reduces disk reads.

subtopics.title: Important Terms
subtopics.theory:
📌 Important Terms Definitions



Durability

Data survives crashes.



Latency

Time to respond.



Throughput

Requests per second.



Hotspot

Node receiving uneven load.



Anti-Entropy

Background synchronization to repair replicas.



Read Repair

Fixing stale replicas during read.



Hinted Handoff

Temporary write storage for failed nodes.

subtopics.title: Final Interview Summary
subtopics.theory:
🎯 Final Interview Summary

A distributed key-value store achieves scalability and fault tolerance using partitioning, replication, quorum-based consistency, versioning, and LSM-tree storage engines while balancing CAP trade-offs.
